questions.question: On a coordinate grid, four points are plotted: (1, 3), (2, 6), (3, 9) and (4, 12). The x-value is the number of SkyTrain tickets bought and the y-value is the total cost in dollars. Should the four points be joined with a line?
options: No, because tickets are counted, so nothing exists between the points
Yes, because the cost in dollars can be any amount between the points
No, because the graph uses only the first quadrant of the coordinate grid
Yes, because the four points line up exactly on one straight line
questions.explain: Tickets are counted in whole numbers, so the relation is discrete and the points stay as separate dots. Lining up in a straight line does not make a relation continuous; ask whether the in-between x-values make sense.

questions.question: On a coordinate grid, the points (0, 0), (1, 4), (2, 8) and (3, 12) are plotted. The x-value is the number of minutes since a rain barrel started filling and the y-value is the number of litres in it. Should these points be joined?
options: No, because only four readings were taken, so nothing is known in between
Yes, because time is continuous and the barrel has a level at every moment
No, because the litres were recorded only as whole numbers on the grid
Yes, because any four points that go up by the same amount must be joined
questions.explain: Time flows without gaps, so at 1.5 minutes the barrel really does hold 6 L; the relation is continuous and the points are joined. Taking readings only at whole minutes does not make the relation discrete.

questions.question: Two relations are plotted on the same coordinate grid. Graph P has points (1, 1), (2, 2) and (3, 3), where x is the number of loonies in a jar and y is their value in dollars. Graph Q has points (0, 20), (1, 18) and (2, 16), where x is the hours a candle has burned and y is its height in centimetres. Which graph should be drawn as a solid line?
options: Only Graph P, because its value in dollars rises by the same amount each time
Both graphs, because the three points of each one lie on a straight line
Only Graph Q, because burning time takes every value between the hours
Neither graph, because each one shows only three plotted points, not a line
questions.explain: Loonies are counted, so Graph P stays as dots; the candle burns through every fraction of an hour, so Graph Q is continuous and its points are joined. A straight-line pattern alone does not decide it; the type of x-variable does.

questions.question: On a coordinate grid, the points (1, 3), (2, 6), (3, 9), (4, 12) and (5, 15) are plotted. The x-value is the number of friends at a pizza party and the y-value is the number of slices needed. Which pair of words correctly describes this relation and its graph?
options: Continuous, so the points are joined by a solid line
Discrete, but the points are still joined by a solid line
Continuous, but the points are still left as separate dots
Discrete, so the points are left as five separate dots
questions.explain: Friends are counted in whole numbers, so the relation is discrete and its points stay as separate dots; a solid line would claim that 2.5 friends need 7.5 slices. Discrete means dots, continuous means a line.

questions.question: At a farm stand, apples cost $2.50 per kilogram, so the cost follows y = 2.5x, where x is the mass in kilograms and y is the cost in dollars. A table lists x = 1, 2, 3, 4 and the points are plotted. Which statement about the graph is correct?
options: Join the points, because a mass such as 1.6 kg is perfectly possible
Leave them as dots, because the cost goes up in fixed steps of $2.50
Leave them as dots, because only whole kilograms appear in the table
Join the points, because every linear relation is joined with a line
questions.explain: Mass can be any amount, so the relation is continuous and the points are joined even though the table only shows whole kilograms. Money is not what decides it; ask whether the x-variable can take in-between values.

questions.question: In each relation below, x and y are as stated. Which one should be graphed as a solid line?
options: y = 4x, where x is the number of bus tickets bought and y is the cost in dollars
y = 50 − 5x, where x is minutes since a drain opened and y is litres left
y = 3x, where x is the number of students and y is the number of pencils
y = 2x + 1, where x is the number of tables and y is the number of chairs
questions.explain: Minutes flow continuously, so the water level exists at every instant and the graph is a solid line. Tickets, students and tables are all counted, so those three relations are discrete and stay as dots even though each has a constant rate.

questions.question: In each relation below, x and y are as stated. Which one must be graphed as separate dots and NOT joined?
options: y = 20 − 2x, where x is hours a candle burns and y is its height in cm
y = 1.8x, where x is litres of gas pumped and y is the cost in dollars
y = 170x, where x is the number of pucks and y is their mass in grams
y = 15x, where x is seconds since a puck was hit and y is metres travelled
questions.explain: Pucks are counted, so 2.5 pucks has no meaning and the points stay as dots. Hours, litres and seconds can all take in-between values, so those relations are continuous and get a solid line, even the one about money.

questions.question: Ben earns $6 per hour babysitting, so y = 6x, where x is hours worked and y is dollars earned. He plots the points for x = 1, 2, 3, 4 and wants to know what he would earn for 2.5 hours. Which statement is correct?
options: Leave the dots unjoined; 2.5 hours is not in the table, so it cannot be earned
Leave the dots unjoined; dollars are counted, so the relation is discrete
Join the points, but only for this question, since 2.5 was asked about
Join the points; reading between them (interpolation) gives $15 for 2.5 h
questions.explain: Time is continuous, so the points are joined and interpolation between (2, 12) and (3, 18) gives $15 for 2.5 hours. Money being counted in dollars does not make the relation discrete; it is the x-variable, hours, that decides.

questions.question: Maya plots the total cost of Playland passes at $40 each for 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 people, joins the points with a solid line, and reads from the line that 3.5 people would cost $140. What went wrong?
options: She joined the points, but people are counted, so 3.5 people is meaningless
Nothing; the cost rises by the same $40 each time, so joining is correct
Nothing; the cost in dollars can be any amount, so the solid line is correct
She read the line wrongly, since 3.5 people on this line should cost $150
questions.explain: People are counted, so the relation is discrete and the points must stay as dots; a line invents values like 3.5 people that cannot happen. A constant rate or money with cents does not make a relation continuous.

questions.question: Kaito draws two graphs. Graph A shows the cost of a field trip, a flat $200 for the bus plus $5 per student, against the number of students. Graph B shows the water level in a leaking tank, read every 10 minutes, against time. Which graph should get a solid line, and what could he correctly read between two plotted points?
options: Only Graph A; the cost for a group size between two plotted points, by interpolation
Only Graph B; the level at a time between two readings, found by interpolation
Both graphs; each has a constant rate of change, so each one is continuous
Neither graph; readings were only made at set times, so nothing lies in between
questions.explain: Time is continuous, so Graph B is joined and interpolation between readings is valid; students are counted, so Graph A stays as dots even though it has a constant rate of $5. Taking readings every 10 minutes does not make time discrete.

questions.question: A vending machine sells drinks for $2.25 each. Zoe plots the total cost against the number of drinks bought, for 1 to 6 drinks. She says the points should be joined because the cost includes cents, so it is not a whole number. Is she right?
options: Yes; the cost can be any amount of dollars and cents, so the relation is continuous
Yes; the points form a straight line, and straight-line patterns are always joined
No; drinks are counted, so the cost exists only at whole numbers of drinks
No; no relation involving money can ever be drawn as a solid line, whatever x is
questions.explain: Whether to join depends on the x-variable: drinks are counted, so the relation is discrete and stays as dots even though the cost has cents. Money appearing in a relation does not by itself make it continuous or discrete.

questions.question: A downtown parking lot charges a flat $6 for any stay up to 8 hours. Leo plots cost against hours parked and gets the points (1, 6), (2, 6), (3, 6) and so on up to (8, 6), all at the same height. What should he do with these points?
options: Leave them as dots; a horizontal pattern means y never changes, so nothing to join
Leave them as dots; only whole hours were plotted, so half hours are unknown
Join them, because any points that line up are joined no matter what x measures
Join them into a horizontal line; time is continuous, so 2.5 hours also costs $6
questions.explain: Hours parked can be any amount, so the relation is continuous and the points are joined into a solid horizontal line at y = 6. A flat rate still gives a relation; the line is just horizontal, not missing.
